items.why: The passage explicitly says the ambushers are waiting for the commander’s consent, though “act” is slightly broad.
Abishai’s victim is directly identified as the Philistine Ishbi-Benob, not David.
The man of God declared the message, but the question’s pronouns and phrase “message…will happen” are awkward.
The command hierarchy clearly places the 307,500 men under the 2,600 family leaders.
The man explicitly grounds his refusal in the Lord’s command, decisively excluding the offered amount.
Athaliah hears the noise before going to the crowd and sees the king only after arriving.
Zechariah is directly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in the fear of God.
The first covenant expressly includes the Lord, king, and people, unlike the second covenant.
The off-duty companies are specifically assigned to guard the temple for the king, though the surrounding assignments are complex.
The officer is the clear antecedent of “him” and the stated victim of the trampling.
“The news” merely repeats the vague object in the question and does not specify what was reported.
Jehoiada is the active giver; David is mentioned only as the weapons’ former owner.
The summary attributes the four defeats collectively to David and his men, while Jonathan killed only the man described here.
The messenger’s “master” and the following speech identify the king as the person Elisha calls a murderer.
The narrated order clearly places Sibbekai’s killing before Elhanan’s, though “who kills first” is somewhat mechanical.
The letter heading plainly distinguishes Claudius Lysias as writer from Felix as addressee.
The prophecy names Josiah as the one who will sacrifice the priests on the altar.
The king’s quoted scenario clearly places entering the city after capturing those who come out.
The writer explicitly says he ordered Paul’s accusers to present their case to the addressee.
The warning is addressed directly to the man of God from Judah, not to the old prophet speaking.
The men explicitly reject staying or entering the city and decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The seven sons are beaten and then run out, while the possessed man administers the beating.
The Arameans explicitly fear the Hittite and Egyptian kings whom Israel supposedly hired.
The returning group contrasts with the cavalry that continues, though calling them simply “the soldiers” is slightly broad.
Jeroboam’s command “Seize him” clearly targets the man of God.
The passage directly says Jeroboam did not change his evil ways and did appoint priests again.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the people’s plundering of the camp.
After admitting wrongdoing, the men explicitly resolve to report immediately to the royal palace.
The order is addressed to the two centurions, who must prepare the listed detachment.
Elisha’s direct reply is that the officer will see the food but not eat it, though the key’s pronoun is underspecified.
Paul explicitly says the young man has something to tell the commander.
The passage gives the complete three-part list of peoples God helped Uzziah oppose.
The repeated singular “he” makes Uzziah the soil-lover, though the question’s phrasing is slightly unnatural.
Azariah and the other priests follow King Uzziah into the temple and then confront him.
Within the old prophet’s claimed message, “him” clearly refers to the man of God being brought back.
The man of God directly performs the intercession requested by the king.
Mobilizing the army is narrated before marching and laying siege, though the ordering question is elementary.
The narrative states after Uzziah’s burial that Jotham succeeded him as king.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet is explicitly the one who mounts it.
The traveling man of God is the clear victim of the lion, not the prophet who sent him off.
Paul’s intention to leave the next day is explicitly given as the reason he talks until midnight.
The speaking woman says “my son” was cooked first, clearly distinguishing him from the hidden child.
Talking until daylight is the final stated action before Paul leaves.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah having been slain.
After bringing the scrolls together, the practitioners immediately burn them publicly.
The text expressly says Uzziah is eager to leave because the Lord afflicted him, not merely because priests hurry him.
The officer is clearly the victim, but this duplicates the stronger trampling question Q89C41.
The explicit sword command targets anyone following the woman, though she too is subsequently put to death.
The quoted plan unambiguously assigns the other woman’s child to tomorrow.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Evil spirits explicitly leave, but “on the items’ arrival” is unnatural and illnesses could colloquially be said to leave too.
Joash, Ahaziah’s son, is explicitly hidden with his nurse for six years.
The people take Uzziah in order to install him as king, while Amaziah’s death is background rather than the purpose.
The conspirators explicitly ask the Sanhedrin to petition the commander to bring Paul before them.
